chapter: Advice to youth and the art of drumming
title: Stick-throwing and trick drummers: Rastus, Hamp, Jack Powell
summary: Showmanship began in vaudeville; he recalls Rastus of Norman Thomas's Quintet in 1933 and Jack Powell's Musical Kitchen.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Great drummers: who they admired and why

blocks.x: That reminds me of something. Guys that always used to throw the sticks up in the air.

Well, that started years ago. It was -- that was called showmanship. And in 1933, I worked with a show, and this act had been on RKO and it was one of the biggest acts in the country, called Norman Thomas' Quintet. And they had this little drummer they called Rastus, and he was about -- oh, I guess he was about four-something feet, and

weighed about 85 pounds. Real, real little bitty guy, but, oh, was he agile. And he would take the sticks and he would juggle them, do four and five -- you know they used to have the thing where they'd put them on the ground.

Right, Hamp does it, right. Five, six sticks and throwing them up in the air and all of this, and he would be doing that. And then they had a finale in the act, and he would -- see, the drummer in the pit would have to keep the time going, because he was just a trick drummer and he would jump up and hit the cymbals and all, and jump up in the chair and up and down and all of this kind of thing. And then he would run to the edge of the stage and run all across the stage, and then slide.

And they had a pit -- I mean, at the end of the pit there, he had a cymbal and he would hit the cymbal and it was right over the head of the pit drummer. And one day he hit some powder or something on the stage and he went right down into the drums.

Yeah, so -- but he was one of the trick drummers. And then they had Jack Powell. I don't -- do you remember him? And they called it his Musical Kitchen. And he was a drummer, and he had all of the pots and the pans and all of this type of thing. He was a white drummer, tremendous. Jack Powell.
This was all on the vaudeville circuit, during the vaudeville days. And he -- I caught him a lot of times.
